blocks.content: Imagine a huge city where every building's real address is a long, complicated number. No one remembers those numbers, so people use simple names instead, and something behind the scenes translates the name into the real address the moment it is needed.

DNS works exactly the same way for the internet. You type a name like a domain, DNS finds the real numerical address behind it, an IP address, and only then does your device actually connect. This topic covers DNS's distributed hierarchy, the full resolution process, the record types it stores, TTL and caching trade-offs, and where DNS shows up as a genuine system design tool, not just a background utility.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273606648-970739467.png
blocks.alt: DNS translates the simple name you type into the real numerical address your device actually needs

blocks.content: DNS is the internet's phone book. You hand it a name, it gives you back the number. Without it, every application would need to hardcode IP addresses, and changing a single server would break every client depending on it.
1. A Distributed Hierarchy, Not One Giant Database
blocks.text: 1. A Distributed Hierarchy, Not One Giant Database

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024509-999613702.png
blocks.alt: No single server knows every domain, responsibility is split across three distinct layers

blocks.content: DNS is a distributed, hierarchical database. No single server anywhere knows every domain in existence. Instead, responsibility is divided across three layers. Root name servers do not know a domain's exact IP, but they know exactly where to find the servers responsible for a given top level domain, .com, .io, .in. Those top level domain servers, in turn, know exactly which authoritative server actually holds the real records for one specific domain.
So the flow is always the same shape, root points to the right TLD servers, TLD points to the right authoritative servers, and the authoritative servers finally return the actual answer.
2. Full DNS Resolution, Step by Step
blocks.text: 2. Full DNS Resolution, Step by Step

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273610748-293419094.png
blocks.alt: Most lookups never touch the network at all, they are answered entirely from a local cache

blocks.content: Looking up a domain for the very first time travels through every layer of the hierarchy, but every lookup after that is usually served from cache long before it ever needs to.

["The browser checks its own DNS cache first, and the operating system checks its own system-wide cache right after, if a still-valid answer exists at either layer, resolution stops immediately","If neither has a valid answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver, often run by an ISP or a public provider, whose entire job is to walk the hierarchy on the client's behalf","The resolver asks a root server, which points it to the correct top level domain servers","The resolver then asks those TLD servers, which point it to the domain's own authoritative servers","The authoritative servers finally return the real answer, which the resolver caches and hands back to the original client"]
items: The browser checks its own DNS cache first, and the operating system checks its own system-wide cache right after, if a still-valid answer exists at either layer, resolution stops immediately
If neither has a valid answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver, often run by an ISP or a public provider, whose entire job is to walk the hierarchy on the client's behalf
The resolver asks a root server, which points it to the correct top level domain servers
The resolver then asks those TLD servers, which point it to the domain's own authoritative servers
The authoritative servers finally return the real answer, which the resolver caches and hands back to the original client

blocks.content: 3. DNS Record Types

DNS does not only store IP addresses. A domain's zone file, the configuration describing exactly how that domain should behave, contains several distinct record types, each serving a genuinely different purpose.

{"headers":["Record","Maps","Common Use"],"rows":[["A","Domain to IPv4 address","The primary record pointing a domain straight at a server"],["AAAA","Domain to IPv6 address","The same idea as A, for IPv6"],["CNAME","Domain to another domain","Aliasing one domain to another, common with CDNs"],["MX","Domain to mail servers","Where email for this domain should actually be delivered"],["TXT","Domain to arbitrary text","Domain ownership verification and security policy declarations"],["NS","Domain to its authoritative servers","Declares which servers are authoritative for this domain"]]}

Together, these records form the complete blueprint of a domain's entire DNS setup, not just where its website lives, but where its email goes and which servers are allowed to speak for it authoritatively.

A misconfigured or missing record in this zone file is a genuinely common cause of a seemingly unrelated production problem, an app that resolves fine but whose transactional emails silently vanish is very often nothing more than a missing or wrong MX record, not a bug in the application sending them at all.
4. TTL and DNS Caching
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273612690-904462202.png
blocks.alt: TTL is a direct trade-off between fewer repeated lookups and how quickly a change actually reaches every client

blocks.content: Every DNS record carries a TTL, Time To Live, in seconds. Resolvers and browsers cache an answer for exactly that long, and until it expires, no fresh DNS query happens at all, the cached answer is used directly.

A high TTL means better caching and less DNS traffic, but changes propagate slowly, if a server goes down or its IP changes, users can keep hitting the old, now dead answer for hours. A low TTL means changes propagate quickly, but clients re-query far more often, adding real, continuous load to the DNS infrastructure at scale.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024987-563921930.png
blocks.alt: Production systems deliberately lower TTL before a planned change and raise it back again once the change is safely complete

blocks.title: The Real Production Pattern
blocks.content: Keep TTL comfortably high, commonly 300 to 3600 seconds, during ordinary operation. A few hours before a planned migration or IP change, lower it to something like 60 seconds so the change propagates to every client quickly. Once the migration is confirmed stable, raise it back to its normal value.
5. CNAME vs A Record
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273616423-177615458.png
blocks.alt: An A record resolves directly to an IP in one step, a CNAME points to another domain that must itself be resolved further

blocks.content: An A record is direct, it maps a domain straight to an IP in a single step. A CNAME instead points to another domain name, not an IP at all, the resolver follows that pointer and keeps resolving until it eventually reaches a genuine A record. This extra indirection is exactly how CDNs commonly work, your own domain CNAMEs to the CDN provider's own domain, which resolves to whichever edge server is actually closest to the requester.

That extra hop does cost a small amount of additional resolution time on an uncached lookup, though it is rarely noticeable in practice once caching takes over, the real value of the indirection is letting the CDN provider change its own underlying servers freely without your own domain's configuration ever needing to change at all.

blocks.title: A Genuine Restriction
blocks.content: A CNAME cannot be used on a domain's own root, only on a subdomain. For the root domain itself, DNS providers offer special records, often called ALIAS or ANAME, that behave like a CNAME to the outside world while still ultimately returning a plain IP address underneath.
6. DNS for Internal Service Discovery
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273618191-348404382.png
blocks.alt: Services call each other by a stable name, letting the actual underlying pods scale up or down freely without anyone noticing

blocks.content: Inside a Kubernetes cluster, every service gets its own DNS name, something like payments-service.production.svc.cluster.local. When order-service calls payments-service by that name, the cluster's own internal DNS resolves it to a stable virtual IP representing the service as a whole, not any one specific pod.

This is exactly why nothing ever hardcodes a pod's own IP address, pods can scale up, scale down, crash, and get replaced constantly, and the service name in front of them never changes, so every caller keeps working without needing to know or care how many actual instances exist behind it at any given moment.
7. DNS as a Naive Load Balancer
blocks.text: 7. DNS as a Naive Load Balancer

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273619828-892132588.png
blocks.alt: Returning several A records for one domain spreads different clients across different servers with zero application-layer logic involved

blocks.content: A domain can have multiple A records pointing at different servers at once. When a client asks DNS to resolve it, it gets back the same set of IPs, just in a rotated order, so different clients tend to connect to different servers first, a crude but genuinely functional form of load distribution requiring no dedicated load balancer at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273621554-749242665.png
blocks.alt: DNS itself has no concept of a server being unhealthy, it will keep handing out a dead server's IP indefinitely

blocks.content: DNS-based load balancing has no health checking built in whatsoever. A dead server keeps receiving its share of traffic until someone manually updates the record, and even then, only once every client's own cached TTL finally expires. Always pair DNS round-robin with genuine health checking somewhere in the actual request path, never rely on it alone.
8. GeoDNS: Routing by Location
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025330-442182283.png
blocks.alt: The exact same domain name resolves to a different, geographically closer server depending on where the request came from

blocks.content: GeoDNS extends the basic idea of multiple A records with actual awareness of where a request is coming from. The same domain resolves to a different answer depending on the requester's approximate location, a visitor in India receiving a server in Mumbai, a visitor in Germany receiving one in Frankfurt, cutting real network latency simply by answering the DNS query itself more intelligently, before a single byte of the actual request has even been sent.

Unlike anycast, covered next, GeoDNS still relies on ordinary A records, it simply chooses which one to hand back based on where the resolver's own request appears to originate from, making it a comparatively simple addition on top of infrastructure a team may already have in place.
9. Anycast: One IP, Many Locations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273624907-764554988.png
blocks.alt: The exact same IP address is announced from many physical locations at once, and ordinary internet routing sends each visitor to whichever one is nearest

blocks.content: Anycast takes a different approach entirely, the very same IP address is announced from many physically separate locations simultaneously, and the internet's own routing infrastructure, not DNS, decides which announcing location a given visitor actually reaches, almost always whichever one is topologically closest. Large public DNS resolvers and content delivery networks rely heavily on anycast specifically so that a single, memorable IP transparently serves an entire global network of physical locations.
10. DNSSEC: Preventing Spoofed Responses
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273626540-150071211.png
blocks.alt: A digitally signed DNS response lets a resolver confirm it genuinely came from the real authoritative source, not an attacker

blocks.content: Ordinary DNS responses carry no proof of who actually sent them, which makes DNS spoofing, an attacker injecting a fake response redirecting a domain to a malicious server, a genuine, real world attack. DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS responses, letting a resolver verify a response genuinely came from the real authoritative chain for that domain, rejecting anything that fails that check rather than trusting it blindly.
11. Reverse DNS: Going From IP Back to Name
blocks.text: 11. Reverse DNS: Going From IP Back to Name

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273628190-917894609.png
blocks.alt: A PTR record answers the opposite question an ordinary A record does, given an IP, what hostname is behind it

blocks.content: Ordinary DNS answers what is the IP for this name. Reverse DNS answers the opposite question, given this IP address, what hostname is behind it, through a dedicated record type called a PTR record. Mail servers commonly check this during spam filtering, an incoming mail server whose IP has no matching, sensible PTR record is treated as a stronger signal of potentially unwanted mail.
12. Split-Horizon DNS
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025564-833619020.png
blocks.alt: The exact same domain name can resolve to a completely different answer depending on whether the query came from inside or outside the company's own network

blocks.content: Split-horizon DNS serves a different answer for the same domain name depending on where the query originates. A company's internal tools might resolve internal.company.com to a private, internal IP address only reachable from within its own network, while queries for the exact same name from the public internet either fail entirely or resolve to a different, public facing address, letting one domain name serve two entirely different purposes for two entirely different audiences.
13. DNS Over HTTPS and DNS Over TLS
blocks.text: 13. DNS Over HTTPS and DNS Over TLS

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273631721-982832127.png
blocks.alt: An ordinary DNS query is plain text and readable by anyone on the network path, DoH and DoT encrypt that same query

blocks.content: An ordinary DNS query travels as plain text, meaning anyone on the network path, an internet provider, a public WiFi operator, can see exactly which domains a device is looking up, even without ever seeing the actual content of the traffic that follows. DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS both encrypt the query itself, closing that specific privacy gap, at the cost of making split-horizon and network-level DNS filtering, both genuinely useful in some contexts, considerably harder to implement.
14. Negative Caching
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273633327-437543383.png
blocks.alt: A failed lookup for a domain that genuinely does not exist is cached too, so the same failure is not repeated needlessly

blocks.content: Caching is not only for successful answers. A query for a domain that genuinely does not exist returns an NXDOMAIN response, and that failure itself is cached for a period too, negative caching, preventing the exact same doomed lookup from being repeated over and over in a short window, which matters in practice for things like a misconfigured client accidentally hammering a nonexistent hostname.
15. A Common Mistake: Trusting DNS Round-Robin Alone
blocks.text: 15. A Common Mistake: Trusting DNS Round-Robin Alone

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025332-362485385.png
blocks.alt: A team that relies purely on DNS round-robin discovers a crashed server keeps receiving traffic long after it should have been pulled from rotation

blocks.content: A recurring, entirely avoidable production incident is treating DNS round-robin as if it were a genuine, health-aware load balancer. It has no idea whether a server is actually alive, it just rotates through whatever records exist. When one server crashes, some fraction of users keep being routed straight to it until a human manually removes that record and every client's own cache finally expires, a real, visible outage for exactly the users unlucky enough to be pointed at the dead server.
16. A Common Mistake: Leaving TTL High Before a Migration
blocks.text: 16. A Common Mistake: Leaving TTL High Before a Migration

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025330-209621934.png
blocks.alt: Migrating a server's IP without first lowering its TTL leaves clients stranded on the old, now dead address for hours

blocks.content: Migrating a server to a new IP address without lowering the record's TTL beforehand strands every client still holding the old cached answer, they keep trying to reach an address that no longer serves anything, for as long as their own cache happens to remain valid, sometimes for hours. Lowering the TTL well ahead of a planned migration is a small, deliberate step that turns an otherwise slow, painful cutover into one most users barely notice at all.

The example below simulates exactly this TTL and staleness risk: a resolver caches an answer for a fixed duration, correctly serves that same cached answer for as long as it remains valid, even after the real server has already moved, and only picks up the new, correct answer once the cache genuinely expires.

codes.python:
class DnsCache:
    # A DNS cache: an answer already cached and still within its TTL is served
    # as-is, even if the real, authoritative answer has since changed, exactly
    # the staleness risk a migration needs a lowered TTL to avoid.
    def __init__(self, ttl_seconds):
        self.ttl_seconds = ttl_seconds
        self.cache = {}  # domain -> (ip, expires_at)

    # current_authoritative_ip simulates what the real server's IP actually is right
    # now, which the cache only finds out about the next time it genuinely looks it up.
    def resolve(self, domain, current_time, current_authoritative_ip):
        cached = self.cache.get(domain)
        if cached is not None and cached[1] > current_time:
            return f"t={current_time}: CACHE HIT, returning {cached[0]}"

        self.cache[domain] = (current_authoritative_ip, current_time + self.ttl_seconds)
        return f"t={current_time}: CACHE MISS, fresh lookup returned {current_authoritative_ip}"


def main():
    cache = DnsCache(300)  # 300 second TTL

    print(cache.resolve("api.example.com", 0, "203.0.113.10"))
    print(cache.resolve("api.example.com", 100, "203.0.113.20"))
    print(cache.resolve("api.example.com", 280, "203.0.113.20"))
    print(cache.resolve("api.example.com", 310, "203.0.113.20"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: Worked Example

A team plans to migrate their API server to new infrastructure over the coming weekend. Two days beforehand, they lower the domain's A record TTL from its usual 3600 seconds down to 60 seconds, and wait a full day, longer than the old TTL, to guarantee every resolver's cache worldwide has picked up the shorter value.

Skipping that waiting period would defeat the entire point, a resolver that cached the old, high TTL answer just before the change would still be holding onto it, unaware the domain's own TTL policy had changed at all, exactly the kind of subtle timing detail that separates a smooth migration from a confusing, partial one.

On migration day, they update the A record to point at the new server's IP. Within roughly a minute, the overwhelming majority of traffic is already reaching the new infrastructure, since almost every client's cached answer expires within that same short window. A few days after confirming the new server is stable, they raise the TTL back to its normal 3600 seconds, restoring the lower DNS query volume ordinary operation depends on.
Common Mistakes

["Relying on DNS round-robin alone as a load balancer, with no actual health checking anywhere in the real request path","Migrating a server's IP address without lowering its TTL well ahead of time, stranding cached clients on the old, dead address","Forgetting a CNAME cannot be placed on a domain's own root, and reaching for the wrong record type instead of the special ALIAS or ANAME records built for that case","Treating DNS resolution as instantaneous and free, when a cache miss genuinely means a real round trip through several layers of servers before an answer comes back"]
items: Relying on DNS round-robin alone as a load balancer, with no actual health checking anywhere in the real request path
Migrating a server's IP address without lowering its TTL well ahead of time, stranding cached clients on the old, dead address
Forgetting a CNAME cannot be placed on a domain's own root, and reaching for the wrong record type instead of the special ALIAS or ANAME records built for that case
Treating DNS resolution as instantaneous and free, when a cache miss genuinely means a real round trip through several layers of servers before an answer comes back

blocks.content: Practice

Use a terminal DNS lookup tool against a real, well-known domain, and identify its A record, its TTL, and its mail server records. Then explain, in your own words, exactly what would happen to already-connected clients if that domain's IP changed at this very instant, given the TTL you just observed.

As a second exercise, design a rough GeoDNS setup for a service with servers in Mumbai, Frankfurt, and Virginia, deciding which regions should be routed to which server, and what should happen if the Mumbai server becomes completely unreachable.

As a third exercise, sketch a split-horizon DNS setup for a company with both an internal admin dashboard and a public marketing site sharing the same parent domain, deciding exactly which record should be visible to which audience.
Key Takeaway

DNS is a distributed, hierarchical lookup system, not one central database, resolving a domain by walking from root servers to TLD servers to the domain's own authoritative servers, then caching the answer for exactly as long as its TTL allows. That TTL is a genuine trade-off between caching efficiency and how quickly a real change actually reaches every client, which is why production systems deliberately lower it before a planned migration. Beyond simple name resolution, DNS shows up as a real system design tool too, internal service discovery, naive round-robin load distribution, and geography-aware routing through GeoDNS and anycast, each one still bound by the same caching and trust trade-offs covered throughout this topic.

Treat DNS as infrastructure worth designing deliberately, not a background detail to configure once and forget, since its own caching behavior directly shapes how quickly the rest of a system can actually recover from change.
